conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain and diarrhea. It started a few hours after I ate at a cookout yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. How often are you having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Every 30 minutes or so. And I can see undigested food in the stool. No blood, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I feel a bit feverish, but no chills or shaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You were just discharged a week ago for a Crohn’s flare—does this pain feel different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s sharper. And it’s more in my lower back, kind of like my old kidney stone pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We did a renal ultrasound in the ER—no stones. But we’ll check a CT to be sure nothing’s changed with your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been on prednisone since last time—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the 40 mg daily until you see your GI doctor. We’re not stopping it unless we’re sure this isn’t a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just don’t want to go through another flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can. For now, we’re giving IV fluids and some pain medication to keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back—white count is normal, and markers of inflammation like CRP and ESR are low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good, right? Not a Crohn’s flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Those markers are usually high during a flare. This suggests it’s less likely to be active Crohn’s inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what’s causing the pain and diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still working on that. Your CT is scheduled for tomorrow. But given the timing after the cookout, we’re thinking it could be gastroenteritis—maybe a viral infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like food poisoning? But I only ate a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t take much. Viruses can be very contagious. And with your history, your gut might react more strongly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have results from your CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. There’s no abscess, no obstruction, and no new inflammation. In fact, the area of thickened bowel from your Crohn’s looks better than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The CT confirms it’s not a flare. The pain and diarrhea are likely from a gastrointestinal infection—gastroenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably not. Most cases are viral and get better on their own. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and let your body heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a little broth earlier. Felt okay. Can I eat more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try clear liquids for now—water, broth, ginger ale. We’ll advance slowly. Last time you tried regular food, it caused discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that didn’t go well. How long should I stay on liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until your bowel movements slow down. Then we’ll move to soft, low-residue foods—like toast, rice, applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look better. Kidney function is normal, and you’re not dehydrated anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit better, but still crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing the pain. But the trend is positive. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the prednisone as before—40 mg daily—until you see your GI doctor. They’ll taper it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use loperamide as needed. But focus on hydration and a low-residue diet for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you with a short supply of pain meds, just in case. But call us if you develop fever, chills, or blood in your stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my GI appointment next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stay on track with that. They’ll help manage your Crohn’s and adjust your treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.
